docs.description: an effect registers a listener that no cleanup releases with the same binding
docs.why: `removeEventListener` and friends compare the listener by reference. A cleanup that passes a freshly-built function — `throttle(onScroll, 100)` evaluated a second time, an inline arrow, a `.bind()` — silently removes nothing, and so does an effect with no cleanup at all. Every re-run then adds another live listener that keeps the render it captured alive. The engine reports `none-seen` when it cannot see a teardown holding the *same* binding, which is the fact that matters: matching the teardown function's *name* would certify the very bug this rule exists to catch.
docs.fix: Bind the listener to a `const` inside the setup, register that name, and pass the same name to the teardown. If the listener is wrapped (`throttle`, `debounce`, `.bind`), wrap once into the binding — never inline the wrapper at both ends.
docs.example:
window.addEventListener('scroll', throttle(onScroll, 100));
return () => window.removeEventListener('scroll', throttle(onScroll, 100));  // different function

docs.description: an effect registers a repeating callback and returns no teardown on any path
docs.why: A repeating registration (`setInterval`, `addEventListener`, `subscribe`) outlives the effect run that created it. With no teardown at all, every re-run — every deps change, every remount, and the StrictMode double-invoke — stacks another live registration, and the old ones keep firing against a component the user has navigated away from. Only the total absence of a teardown is provable here: an effect that returns a cleanup on *some* paths reads as `present` and is not flagged.
docs.fix: Return a function from the setup that undoes the registration, on every path that performed one. If the registration is conditional, hoist the condition above it (`if (!enabled) return;`) so the acquiring path always has a matching teardown.

docs.description: an effect schedules a one-shot continuation (`.then`, `setTimeout`) and returns no teardown that could cancel it
docs.why: A continuation scheduled by the setup runs after the effect has already been torn down — the user navigated away, or the deps changed and a newer run is in flight. With no cleanup, this run has nothing that can flip a cancellation token or abort a signal, so the late continuation writes state for a mount nobody sees, and two overlapping runs can both write the same slot with whichever response lands last winning. The built-in `missing-cleanup` deliberately skips one-shot registrars, so this shape is otherwise unreported.
docs.fix: Return a cleanup from the setup and have the continuation consult it: a `let cancelled = false` declared *inside the setup* (one per run, unlike a `useRef`, which is one per mount and cannot tell run k from run k+1), or an `AbortController` whose signal is passed to the request and aborted by the cleanup.

rules.message: this effect schedules a one-shot continuation and returns no teardown — nothing can cancel it when the effect re-runs or unmounts

docs.description: an effect whose only inputs are state slots writes another state slot and touches nothing external
docs.why: This is one link of a cascading effect chain: a prop change updates slot A, an effect turns A into B, another turns B into C. Each link costs an extra commit, and between commits the browser paints a frame where A is already new and B still describes the previous data — the summary flashes the old number. The built-in `derived-state` catches the links whose right-hand side is call-free; this rule extends to links that call a helper (`setTotals(computeTotals(rows))`), which `derived-state` lets through.
docs.fix: Compute the value during render — `const totals = computeTotals(rows)` — or `useMemo` it if it is expensive, and delete the state slot. Do this from the end of the chain backwards; each removal usually exposes the next.

rules.message: this effect only turns state into state — it writes {setter.slot} from deps that are all state slots, costing an extra commit
